newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen to continue acquisitions strategy.
newsitem.headline: Loewen to continue acquisitions strategy.

text.p: Loewen Group Inc said it will continue to pursue its aggressive growth strategy in 1997 after buying a record number of funeral homes and cemeteries last year.
Loewen also said it was pleased that North America's largest funeral home operator, Service Corp. International, had dropped its $2.9 billion hostile bid for the company.

"Today's announcement is good news for the industry, Loewen Group shareholders and consumers. Our company has performed strongly throughout 1996, and with this distraction behind us, we look forward to continued implementation of our growth strategy in 1997," Chairman and chief executive Raymond Loewen said in a statement on Tuesday.

Loewen, based in Vancouver, British Columbia, is Houston-based Service Corp.'s biggest rival. The company has survived several near-death experiences over the past year, including a brush with bankruptcy.

Service cited Loewen's recent acquisition program, costs associated with Loewen's executive severance packages and uncertainties about divestitures that might be required to complete the transaction as reasons for dropping its bid, but Loewen later said it disagreed with these reasons.

"The Loewen Board of Directors has consistently stated that the SCI proposal was inadequate and that the best way to maximise value for shareholders is through the continued implementation of the company's superior long-term business plan as an independent company," Loewen said in a press release.

Loewen also said last month that the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, the Canadian Competition Bureau and officials in several U.S. states had launched investigations into the potential antitrust implications of a deal.
The company said that in 1996 its funeral home and cemetery acquisitions reached a record level and the aggressive pace of acquisition activity would continue this year.
It said it was involved in acquisitions or structured transactions totaling $1.4 billion last year.
In 1996, Loewen Group signed or closed acquisition deals worth a record $830 million, compared with $795 million the previous year, the company said.

It said it was also involved in two major transactions with Blackstone Capital Partners II Merchant Banking Fund L.P. to buy Prime Succession Inc. of Batesville, Indiana, North America's fourth-largest supplier of funeral services, for $295 million and Rose Hills cemetery and related mortuary of Los Angeles, the largest cemetery in North America, for $240 million.
"I am very optimistic about our ability to continue to build shareholder value in the future as we execute the Loewen Group's growth plans," Loewen said.
Earlier on Tuesday analysts said any elation felt by Loewen was likely to be tempered by a swift drop in the company's stock price on Wednesday, which they put at five to 15 percent.
But they said that Loewen's stock should attract buying interest after an initial sell-off.

Loewen is the second-largest funeral home and cemetery operator in North America after Service. It owns about 951 funeral homes and 299 cemeteries in the United States and Canada with about 90 percent of its revenue coming from U.S. operations.

Service Corp. had 2,864 funeral service locations, 335 cemeteries and 147 crematoria worldwide as of September 30. It provides funeral and cemetery services in North America, Europe and the Pacific Rim.
